vignette:
Eleanor had spent her life under the open sky. As an environmental scientist, she had charted wetlands and catalogued prairie grasses, feeling more at home in the vast, exposed landscapes of the Midwest than in any room with four walls. At seventy-seven, even in semi-retirement, she still consulted on local conservation projects. It was at one such event, a park cleanup she was leading, that her world contracted to the size of a single, terrifying moment. A man she vaguely knew from the neighborhood, a fellow volunteer, had offered to help her carry a heavy box of equipment to her car. She’d accepted with a grateful smile. The attack happened in the quiet, tree-lined corner of the parking lot, a space that was both open and inescapable.

In the months that followed, Eleanor’s sense of the world fundamentally shifted. She began to operate under the assumption of imminent danger, a state of high alert that became her new baseline. At home, she found herself listening intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, her body rigid until she could identify the groan of the pipes or the settling of the foundation. Out in the world, any sudden movement from a passerby would cause her to flinch, her heart hammering against her ribs. Living at this pitch of alertness, she found that once-innocent social cues had become charged with potential harm; a friendly touch or the simple presence of a man in a quiet room now registered as immediate warnings. This constant, exhausting vigilance served as a running commentary, confirming the beliefs that were taking root in her mind. Each startled jump was proof that you can never truly know who will harm you; each moment spent scanning her surroundings reinforced the terrible conclusion that she had to be this watchful now because she had failed to be watchful then.

This pervasive sense of threat dictated her every action. She had always prided herself on her directness, but now she found she could no longer make eye contact with people, especially men, as if looking away might render her invisible. The open spaces she once cherished now felt menacingly exposed. During a recent consulting visit to a nature preserve, she found herself unable to leave the wooded path to walk into the meadow she was meant to be assessing, a profound sense of vulnerability rooting her to the spot. Her life became a series of logistical calculations; before entering a grocery store or even the local library, she would first identify all possible escape routes, her mind mapping exits before she could allow her body to feel settled.

These strategies, meant to keep her safe, instead became the architecture of her prison. By avoiding the open fields, she never had the chance to learn that she could be safe there, leaving the fear unchallenged and absolute. Her constant rumination, replaying the assault and meticulously listing all the ways she could have prevented it—by not being so friendly, by refusing the offer of help—was a form of self-flagellation that cemented her corrosive self-blame. Each time she averted her gaze from a kind stranger, she reinforced the belief that the world was hostile and that she was right to be afraid. This, in turn, kept her nervous system on a hair trigger, ensuring that her sense of being under constant threat never abated.

Her deeply held belief that the assault was her own fault, a consequence of her own actions, made everyday interactions feel fraught with danger. Because she blamed her own trusting nature, any expression of affection became a potent trigger. A friendly hand on her arm or a well-meaning hug would send a jolt of panic through her, feeling like a terrifying echo of the prelude to the attack. Her conviction that you can never know who will harm you transformed the simple presence of a man in an elevator or a quiet room into an unbearable source of anxiety. The shame she felt about what had happened to her body made any depiction of intimacy on television, let alone the thought of it in her own life, a source of visceral revulsion.

Eleanor came to therapy after her seven-year-old grandson ran to hug her and she recoiled so sharply that he stumbled backward and began to cry. The sight of his confused, hurt face was the one thing that could cut through the fog of her fear. Her world had become small and airless, and she had begun to poison the lives of those she loved most. She wants to be able to hold her grandson again, to walk in a meadow without terror, but she is deeply afraid that the belief now lodged in her bones—that safety is an illusion she was once foolish enough to believe in—is the only truth left.
